title: AI writes a balance change for my roguelite in minutes. Proving it’s right takes forever. How do you test balance?
author: vizyn
selftext:
I'm a solo dev making a roguelite; I've spent the majority of my time with this game trying to balance it and it has been a grind to say the least.

As the title says writing balance changes is now cheap, but identifying and proving a change is the right call is still expensive.

**Why this game is hard to balance**

- **There's no "perfect play" to measure against.** "Hitless" is not a realistic goal for a run, and while mechanical execution still matters, you're mostly forced to minimize losses rather than prevent them.
- **The same seed doesn't give the same run.** Two runs from one seed drift apart within minutes, so I can't test a change by replaying a seed before and after. I have to average many runs: about 75 before I can tell a change moved bots even half a biome further.
- **It's slow.** Even drawing nothing, a game runs at about 2x real time, because the cost is simulating many thousands of units, not rendering them. I can get 10 to 20 bot runs an hour on my machine, so one A/B question takes 4 to 8 hours.
- **Bots aren't people.** I've done my best to simulate human-like behavior.  Bots draft upgrades with many different strategies.  Claude models bots after the playtest data from the limited play-testers I've had.. but it isn't enough.

**What I've tried**

- Bots can A/B a change without a rebuild because I've made every adjustable value a knob set through env vars.
- A roster of bots (different drafting styles and reaction speeds) run overnight. I capture every draft option and decision as well as damage done/damage taken/growth/etc.. 
- Each run saves a checkpoint at every boss, so a boss change replays only that fight.
- Player runs come back in the same format as bot runs, so I can put them side by side.

**How has it gone?**

For my personal playtest experience the needle is moving in the right direction.. just slowly.  For others.. even with limited play-testers the results have an incredibly large range.  From one who skipped the tutorial and won their first run to someone who did the tutorial and fully tried to engage with the game but couldn't make it out of the first biome after 4 attempts.

**What I'd love your take on**

1. First, how do you define your targets when player ability can range so drastically?
2. Has anyone scaled sim-heavy Unity bot runs out to cloud machines? Did true headless (-batchmode -nographics) buy you much over just not drawing?
3. How do you make a bot play like a first-timer and not like a script? Has anyone trained one from player telemetry, or put an LLM in the drafting seat?
4. With noisy runs and few play-testers, what gets you the most signal per run?

Would truly value any feedback/suggestions on ways to shorten my cycle time and improve my process.

I'm using Opus 5.5 for all of the relevant work discussed in this post.

comments.author: StoneCypher

comments.author: IndianaNetworkAdmin
comments.body:
I was as putting together an incremental strategy game. I had opus put together a number of personality traits and then it fed those to glm 5.3 flash instances as well as deep seek flash. I then had them play the game multiple times on a higher speed. They recorded the results such as how much in-game time passed before they took their first province, created their first army, made their first research decision. It also tracked their economy over time, their victory and failure rate in battle etc. Finally, it put together a list of possible causes and balance changes based on those results.

For later stages of game play, I had them save the game on the first playthroughs so that I didn't have to retest the first part of the game. I then had a dozen starting points and ran then each by every personality type for more results.

Because it's mainly a numbers game, it didn't have to run the full game in a UI, it was able to do it in a headless mode. It only had to spin up the visible UI to confirm actual UI changes. 

I also used this data to map out the artificial intelligence opponents. I'm going to have traditional AI opponents, but I'm also considering having a very small decision model ship with the game to try and add some variation in personality.

comments.author: nsjames1
comments.body:
Sounds like you're muddling two different things together. You probably have the gameplay engine deeply intertwined with the game runner. Which means anytime you want to check the logic you have to run the actual game. 

The proper way to design this is that you have the logic running at its own layer that can be imported into the game, and then the assets and the runner using those components/services. 

That way you can simulate the logic very very quickly without having to run the actual gameplay.

replies.author: vizyn
replies.body: You aren't wrong, but logic is 50-66% of the main-thread frame time.

comments.author: caster
comments.body:
Have you tried personally playing your game and deciding what level of challenge is appropriate?

"Balance" is a very, very over-used word when players are often talking about design or difficulty or other topics. How hard is this challenge supposed to be? How long do you intend for it to take, including failures/retries? How punishing do you want to be of mistakes; does one mistake mean failure, or ten? Requiring "perfect play" is probably too high a level of challenge, especially if the duration of this challenge is long.

Coding agents don't have the understanding of games that you do from *playing* them. They see the games' guts and can produce more guts. But they have no idea what *playing the game* is like at all, and cannot help you at all when it comes to this type of question, so you are going to have to just make a decision and tell Opus what you want it to do.

replies.author: vizyn
replies.body:
Maybe I made it unclear in my post because you're the second person that suggested I'm trying to tell the AI to balance my game.  I'm not.  I'm trying to optimize my cycle time in collecting data through bot runs, making decisions, and validating those decisions against their impact on the game.

Yes, I've personally played my game many, many times.  It's a roguelite, and so some failure is expected while the player learns the mechanics, enemies, upgrade decisions, etc..  I, however, have a deep understanding of how to play optimally and what each decision means for my run.  The difficulty is reducing cycle time on changes I identify and make, verifying they accomplish what my intent was and don't have unintended consequences that impact other systems.

replies.author: caster
replies.body:
Without knowing more about the game it's hard to come up with a specific strategy for how to do what you want.

But if we suppose you were making a Slay the Spire type game, one approach you might consider is to have "bot strategy" tests where you assign a bot playthrough run a strategy that it will use, and then see how it does following that procedure for how to play.

Obviously a bot is unlikely to be as good as a human player, but it might be better than a rookie player who doesn't understand the game yet. If your deterministic bot strategy is consistently reaching a certain point in the roguelike run that suggests that strategy is good enough to reach that point in the campaign.

For example, let's say you are simulating a bot strategy of an Ironclad run using Juggernaut builds, and when there are three acts this bot strategy usually gets somewhere in Act 2 before dying.

Your first calibration step is probably being able to beat the game yourself using a particular strategy, and then after you've done that you can develop a bot strategy decision tree to make an automated run (perhaps headless) to do the same thing and see how effective it is. With a selection of different bot strategies in the test battery you can decide how far each should be going.
